    21.1Recommended choices (as of late 2026)#

    I need to… Use Notes
    Encrypt data with a shared key AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 XChaCha20-Poly1305 if you want random nonces; AES-GCM-SIV if nonce reuse is a risk
    Encrypt a file age, or GnuPG Don't use openssl enc for real data (no integrity)
    Hash data (integrity, fingerprints) SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3, BLAKE2/BLAKE3
    Authenticate a message with a shared key HMAC-SHA256 Or use AEAD, which includes authentication
    Store user passwords Argon2id scrypt or bcrypt are fine; PBKDF2 (600,000+ iterations) if FIPS is required
    Turn a shared secret into keys HKDF Never use raw key-exchange output directly
    Agree on a key X25519, ideally hybrid X25519MLKEM768 ECDH P-256 where required
    Sign data Ed25519, or ECDSA P-256 RSA-PSS 3072+ where RSA is required; ML-DSA for post-quantum
    Encrypt to someone's public key HPKE (RFC 9180), age, or RSA-OAEP 3072+ Hybrid encryption under the hood
    Generate random values The OS CSPRNG (secrets, crypto.getRandomValues, /dev/urandom) Never random / Math.random
    Secure network connections TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 with ECDHE + AEAD only if needed)
    Website certificates ECDSA P-256 (or RSA 2048+), automated via ACME Serve the full chain; set CAA; monitor CT
    Remote login SSH with Ed25519 keys (or ed25519-sk hardware keys) Disable password login on servers
    VPN WireGuard, or IPsec IKEv2
    Hide who you're talking to Tor (with HTTPS inside it) A VPN only moves the trust to one provider (Chapter 20)
    Wi-Fi WPA3 (WPA2-AES if necessary) with a long passphrase Disable WPS
    User logins Passkeys, or password + phishing-resistant MFA SMS only as a last resort
    "Sign in with…" another account, or app access to an account OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0: authorization code flow + PKCE Never the implicit flow; validate ID tokens and redirect URIs (Chapter 20)
    Messaging Signal Protocol / MLS-based apps with E2EE on by default
    Long-term secrets (10+ years) AES-256 and post-quantum key exchange now "Harvest now, decrypt later"
    ✔ section read

    21.2Avoid#

    ❌ Don't use Why Use instead
    DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish (for new systems) Broken or small blocks AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305
    ECB mode Leaks patterns GCM
    CBC/CTR without a MAC Malleable; padding oracles AEAD
    MD5, SHA-1 Collisions SHA-256, SHA-3
    Fast hashes for passwords Billions of guesses per second Argon2id
    RSA under 2048 bits Factorable RSA 3072+ or ECC
    RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption Padding oracle attacks OAEP, HPKE
    Textbook RSA Deterministic and malleable Proper padding / libraries
    SSL 2/3, TLS 1.0/1.1 Known attacks TLS 1.3 / 1.2
    Static RSA key exchange No forward secrecy ECDHE / X25519
    OAuth implicit flow, or OAuth without PKCE Tokens leak through URLs; stolen codes can be redeemed Authorization code flow + PKCE
    WEP, WPA (TKIP), PPTP Broken WPA3, WireGuard
    Dual_EC_DRBG, home-made RNGs Backdoored or weak OS CSPRNG
    Home-made algorithms or protocols Unreviewed Standard libraries and protocols
    ✔ section read

    21.4OpenSSL command cheat sheet#

    All commands were tested with OpenSSL 3.6.

    Terminal
    # ---------- Randomness ----------
openssl rand -hex 32                                    # 256-bit random value (hex)
openssl rand -base64 24                                 # random password-like string

# ---------- Hashing and HMAC ----------
openssl dgst -sha256 file.txt
printf 'hello' | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "secret"

# ---------- Encoding (NOT encryption) ----------
printf 'Hello' | openssl base64
echo 'SGVsbG8=' | openssl base64 -d                    # needs a trailing newline, hence echo

# ---------- Symmetric file encryption (learning only; no integrity) ----------
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -salt -in in.txt -out out.enc
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in out.enc

# ---------- Key generation ----------
openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out rsa.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out ec.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out ed.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm X25519 -out x.key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-KEM-768 -out mlkem.key   # OpenSSL 3.5+
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out mldsa.key    # OpenSSL 3.5+
openssl pkey -in rsa.key -pubout -out rsa.pub           # extract public key
openssl pkey -in rsa.key -text -noout                   # inspect a key

# ---------- Public-key encryption (RSA-OAEP) ----------
openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pubin -inkey rsa.pub -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:oaep \
  -pkeyopt rsa_oaep_md:sha256 -in msg.txt -out msg.enc
openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey rsa.key -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:oaep \
  -pkeyopt rsa_oaep_md:sha256 -in msg.enc

# ---------- Key exchange ----------
openssl pkeyutl -derive -inkey my_x.key -peerkey their_x.pub -out shared.bin

# ---------- Signatures ----------
openssl pkeyutl -sign   -inkey ed.key -rawin -in doc.txt -out doc.sig            # Ed25519
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey ed.pub -rawin -in doc.txt -sigfile doc.sig
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign rsa.key -out doc.sig doc.txt                          # RSA / ECDSA
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify rsa.pub -signature doc.sig doc.txt

# ---------- Certificates ----------
openssl req -new -key server.key -subj "/CN=example.com" -out server.csr          # make a CSR
openssl req -in server.csr -noout -text                                          # inspect a CSR
openssl req -x509 -new -key ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 -subj "/CN=My CA" \
  -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE" -out ca.crt                        # self-signed CA
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -days 90 -sha256 -extfile server-ext.cnf -out server.crt                       # sign a CSR
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -text                                         # inspect a cert
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256
openssl verify -CAfile root.crt -untrusted intermediate.crt server.crt           # check a chain

# ---------- Formats ----------
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform DER -out cert.der                             # PEM → DER
openssl pkcs12 -export -in server.crt -inkey server.key -certfile chain.crt -out bundle.p12

# ---------- Inspect live servers ----------
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -brief </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates
openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert server.crt -key server.key -www              # test server

    21.5Key and output sizes at a glance#

    Thing Size
    AES-128 / AES-256 key 16 / 32 bytes
    AES block 16 bytes
    AES-GCM nonce / tag 12 / 16 bytes
    ChaCha20 key / nonce (XChaCha20 nonce) 32 / 12 (24) bytes
    SHA-256 / SHA-512 output 32 / 64 bytes
    HMAC-SHA256 tag 32 bytes
    X25519 public key / shared secret 32 / 32 bytes
    Ed25519 public key / signature 32 / 64 bytes
    ECDSA P-256 signature ~64–72 bytes
    RSA-2048 / RSA-3072 signature or ciphertext 256 / 384 bytes
    ML-KEM-768 public key / ciphertext 1,184 / 1,088 bytes
    ML-DSA-65 public key / signature 1,952 / 3,309 bytes
    Typical TLS certificate (ECDSA) ~700–1,500 bytes (PEM)

    21.6The whole guide in 15 sentences#

    1. Cryptography protects confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation, even when attackers can see and change everything.
    2. Everything about a good system is public except the key.
    3. Keys must come from a cryptographically secure random number generator.
    4. Symmetric encryption (AES, ChaCha20) is fast and protects the actual data, but both sides need the same key.
    5. Always use authenticated encryption (AEAD), and never reuse a nonce with the same key.
    6. Hashes are one-way fingerprints; MACs are fingerprints with a secret key; signatures are fingerprints anyone can verify but only the key owner can make.
    7. Passwords must be stored with slow, salted, memory-hard hashing like Argon2id.
    8. Public-key cryptography uses a public key and a private key, solving the problem of sharing keys with strangers.
    9. Key exchange (Diffie-Hellman, X25519, ML-KEM) creates a shared secret in public; ephemeral keys give forward secrecy.
    10. Key exchange without authentication is vulnerable to a man in the middle.
    11. Certificates bind public keys to names, vouched for by certificate authorities in a chain of trust.
    12. TLS combines all of the above: key exchange, certificates, signatures, HKDF and AEAD, in one round trip.
    13. The same building blocks power SSH, VPNs, Wi-Fi, Signal, passkeys, disk encryption and cryptocurrencies.
    14. Crypto usually fails through bad randomness, bugs, misconfiguration, stolen keys and people, rarely through broken math, so use well-reviewed libraries and don't roll your own.
    15. Quantum computers threaten today's public-key crypto, and the migration to post-quantum algorithms is already underway.
